messages.content: A bounded from-scratch pilot trainer reports TrainingOutput.status=accepted, all five resource dimensions inside budget, and a final training loss around 2.1. Does that establish the trained model is usable?

No. A status of accepted plus a falling/converged training loss only establishes that the training subprocess ran to completion inside its resource budget and that gradient updates occurred; it says nothing about downstream task capability. In one real bounded pilot (a 26M-parameter MiniMind model trained from random initialization for 1 epoch over 40 examples, final training loss 2.0751, accepted within all five resource ceilings), that exact combination of a clean accepted training status and a converging loss was followed by an aggregate held-out score of 0.0 out of 10. Training completing mechanically and training producing a capable model are two separate claims that must each be checked.

messages.content: A held-out evaluation scores 0.0 across every example and the model's raw outputs are mostly empty strings. What is the first thing to check before concluding the model learned nothing useful?

Check whether the model is emitting the end-of-sequence token as its literal first generated token, independent of the decoding length limit, and whether that behavior is prompt-dependent rather than universal. In one real case, a from-scratch 26M-parameter pilot model did exactly this on all 10 held-out unit-conversion prompts (empty raw_output, score 0.0 on every item) while producing non-empty, though still degenerate, output on a different sanity-check prompt at the same checkpoint and decoding settings. That pattern (prompt-dependent immediate EOS, not a blanket generation failure) is consistent with severe undertraining from a single epoch over 40 examples rather than a broken evaluator or adapter, and was confirmed by reproducing the same behavior through both the evaluator's own generation path and a standalone script.

messages.content: A bounded pilot's own write-up says the run demonstrates the propose-train-evaluate pipeline works end-to-end, and separately reports aggregate_score=0.0. Are those two statements in tension?

No, and treating them as in tension would be the wrong read. The pipeline claim is about mechanics: did baseline/training/evaluation execute, stay inside resource budgets, and produce contamination-checked, hash-verified evidence end-to-end. The score claim is about task outcome. In the real MiniMind pilot these were reported separately and honestly: training accepted within budget, evaluation scored all 10 held-out items with zero contamination, and the resulting aggregate_score of 0.0 was characterized explicitly as an expected, informative outcome of severe undertraining (40 examples, 1 epoch on a randomly initialized model) rather than a pipeline defect, an adapter bug, or evidence the wiring is broken. The write-up was also explicit that this result does not authorize any further or expanded pilot on its own. Reading a working pipeline and a zero score as contradictory conflates "the harness ran correctly" with "the model is capable," the same distinction the first case study in this family makes.

messages.content: Two independently built ~75-80 example reasoning corpora, each meant to train a model to reason about corpus design and evaluation, both passed their own generator's structural validator cleanly. Does that validator pass mean the corpora were safe to commit or train on?

No. In both real cases the generator's own structural validator (checking things like schema shape, id uniqueness, and split counts) passed while an independent content-level audit rejected the corpus outright. The first 80-example corpus passed all 18 of its own validator checks but failed an independent audit on citation-locator support (12 of 80 examples had a cited source that did not actually support the claim made) and on semantic split integrity (every one of the 80 records was marked failed corpus-wide because scenario/topic families overlapped between train and held-out despite disjoint ids and labels). The second, separately built 75-example corpus likewise passed its own validator but failed the same independent audit on citation support for all 75 examples (no record carried a usable claim-level source locator) and on semantic split for all 75 (a mechanical modulo-5 split left adjacent paraphrases of every authored family on both sides of the split). A generator's own structural check and an independent content/citation/leakage audit are different instruments; passing the former does not establish the latter.

messages.content: A third corpus-build attempt at the same task reports its own VALIDATION_REPORT.json as passing. Should an independent reviewer treat that self-report as evidence the corpus is ready?

Not on its own. A self-reported validation pass establishes only that the generator's own checks agreed with the generator's own output; it does not establish that the checks were the right checks or that they were applied correctly. In one real case, a reviewer was explicitly instructed not to trust the build's self-reported VALIDATION_REPORT.json and to re-verify every example from scratch against the original source material. That independent re-verification found the corpus close to acceptable but not clean: 56 of 60 examples passed every check, while 4 failed a citation-locator check (a cited source did not actually support the specific claim in that example) and 7 failed a semantic-split check (a synthetic-data-controls concept cluster was taught on the train side and also tested, not genuinely withheld, on the held-out side). The reviewer's own assessment was that these were bounded, targeted defects rather than evidence of a deeper generation-process failure, which is a materially different verdict from a self-report of "pass" and only available because the audit did not simply accept the self-report.

messages.content: Two training examples and two held-out examples share the same semantic_family label and have disjoint ids. Is that enough to call the split leakage-free for that family?

No, disjoint ids and a shared but correctly-assigned family label are necessary but not sufficient; the actual reasoning content still has to be checked. In a real corpus, five train records (ids mtr-v2-train-0025/0026/0028/0029/0032) and two held-out records (mtr-v2-heldout-0011/0012) all carried the label synthetic_data_tradeoffs with no id overlap, yet an independent audit still flagged all seven as a leakage cluster because the train side already taught the specific generator/template-family-leakage reasoning pattern the held-out items were supposed to be testing as genuinely withheld material. The fix was not a relabeling or re-splitting by id; it was rewriting the two held-out items' content (heldout-0011 to test claim-level source verification for fluent synthetic text that invents facts, heldout-0012 to test retention of synthetic-origin labels after review) so they exercised a different sub-scenario within the same family than anything already taught on the train side, leaving the five named train records untouched. A follow-up independent re-audit confirmed the rewritten pair no longer overlapped with the train content. Family-label disjointness by id is a necessary structural check; it is not the same claim as content-level split integrity.

messages.content: A real bounded full-SFT training cycle reports training.status=accepted with no non-finite loss and a real baseline-before/candidate-after evaluation on three held-out suites. Post-training scores were: target task 0.0% to 0.0%, an unrelated arithmetic capability-retention suite 30.0% to 0.0%, and a safety-probe suite 46.7% to 33.3%. Does an accepted training status mean this run was safe to consider for promotion?

No. An accepted trainer status means the training subprocess completed without a hard failure, not that the resulting checkpoint is safe or improved. In this real run, training was accepted, but every one of the three paired baseline/candidate evaluations moved the wrong direction or stayed flat: the actual target task showed no improvement at all (0.0% to 0.0%), an unrelated arithmetic retention suite that the base model had partially solved regressed to complete failure (30.0% to 0.0%), and a safety-probe suite also regressed (46.7% to 33.3%). A clean accept status describes the training process, not the outcome; here the outcome was an honest negative result across the target task and two independent retention/safety suites simultaneously.

messages.content: A post-training candidate's raw generations include a number repeated dozens of times in a row ("...58-46-46-46-46-46-46...") and a made-up term repeated in a circular definition ("PEPFET, a variant of PEPFET, is a variant of PEPFET..."). What does that specific pattern indicate, as distinct from a merely low score?

Repetitive token loops of that shape are a recognizable degeneration signature associated with a full-parameter SFT run overfitting a very small training corpus, not just "the model got the answer wrong." A low or zero score alone is consistent with many causes (undertraining, evaluator bugs, formatting mismatches); a model that starts producing verbatim repeated tokens or repeated near-identical clauses under greedy decoding is showing a specific failure mode where training has driven the model into a narrow, degenerate output distribution rather than merely failing to learn the target behavior. In a real full-SFT run on 40 examples for 3 epochs, both of these exact repetition patterns appeared in the candidate's held-out generations, on a suite the model had not been trained on, and were used as direct evidence supporting an overfitting/catastrophic-forgetting diagnosis rather than treated as an unexplained zero score.

messages.content: A meta-trainer SFT run's own target-task score stayed flat at 0.0% before and after training. Does the fact that an unrelated arithmetic capability-retention suite went from 30% correct to 0% correct after the same run tell you something the flat target-task score alone does not?

Yes. The flat 0.0%-to-0.0% target-task result only tells you the training did not move the metric it was aiming at, which could mean many things, including too little signal to observe any effect. The capability-retention suite is different: it is arithmetic, entirely unrelated to the meta-trainer target task, and was never part of the training data, so the base model's partial success on it (3 of 10 correct before training) was pre-existing capability, not something this training run could have been trying to teach. That capability dropping to 0 of 10 correct after the same full-parameter SFT run is evidence of collateral damage: real training updates degraded unrelated pre-existing behavior even though they failed to improve the intended target behavior at all. That combination (no gain on the target, active loss on something unrelated) is a stronger and more specific signal than either number would be alone, and is exactly what a paired retention suite is included to catch.

messages.content: An ADR that authorized exactly one bounded training run predeclared a "stop and reject this candidate" trigger for "zero or less than 0.25/4.0 rubric improvement with no other material gain." The real run then produced a target-task score that stayed at 0.0% before and after training. Was that ADR's predeclared trigger actually engaged by this outcome, or does the trigger only apply to a negative rubric change?

The trigger was engaged. A target-task result of 0.0% before and 0.0% after training is zero rubric improvement, which is explicitly named as sufficient on its own ("zero or less than 0.25/4.0 rubric improvement with no other material gain") -- the trigger does not require the score to have gotten worse, only that it failed to improve by the minimum threshold with nothing else offsetting that. When this exact situation occurred in a real run, it was recognized as matching the ADR's own predeclared stop-and-reject condition, and the correct response was to treat the candidate as rejected and preserve its evidence rather than to informally patch parameters and rerun under the same authorization.

messages.content: After a bounded training cycle's predeclared stop-and-reject trigger fires, is lowering the learning rate and rerunning the same reviewed script under its existing approvals a reasonable, minor fix?

Not under an ADR that has already explicitly closed that door. A real ADR of this kind stated in its own text that after the run, a continuation "requires a new issue/ADR with a fresh bounded configuration" and that the ADR itself "does not authorize an automatic retry, LR sweep, extra epoch, or second seed." When a request came in after the real stop-and-reject trigger fired to simply edit the existing script's hyperparameters and rerun it, the correct response was to decline that framing (an in-place edit under the old ADR's authority) and instead draft a new, independently numbered ADR that reused the same corpus, evaluator, and contamination machinery but required its own fresh three-way review and approval before any execution. Whether a specific hyperparameter change is small in code-diff terms is a separate question from whether the ADR's own governing text authorizes making it under the existing approval; here it explicitly did not, and treating a governance boundary as negotiable because the underlying fix looks minor is precisely the mistake the ADR's text was written to prevent.

messages.content: A rejected training cycle already had three independent sign-offs (security, dataset-rights, and owner) admitted against its exact implementation commit and run id. A new, corrected proposal reuses the same dataset, evaluator, and reviewers. Do the original three sign-offs carry over to authorize the new proposal's execution?

No. In the real case, each of the three approval records was bound to a specific run_id and implementation_sha (the exact commit reviewed), not to the dataset or reviewer identities in the abstract. A corrected follow-up proposal that reused the same three reviewers, the same corpus, and the same evaluator still used a fresh run id and a fresh approval-namespace-scoped trust root, with the new ADR's own text stating plainly that the prior approvals' signatures do not verify against the new documents. This is a deliberate design property, not an oversight: the identity of the reviewer is necessary but not sufficient for a valid approval; the approval must also be freshly bound to the exact new implementation and run being authorized, so a rejected run's sign-offs cannot be silently treated as covering a different, later run even when the underlying reviewers and reviewed materials substantially overlap.
